title: Would You Do Me a Favor?

jokes.text: Hank tells the warm-up crowd the sign says 'Apple sauce' then corrects himself to 'Applause'
jokes.setup: Hank is warming up the studio audience and reads the cue card
jokes.punchline: 'Apple sauce. No, no, I'm kidding. It says applause.' — Hank undercuts his own authority as warm-up man with a self-deprecating fake-out
jokes.explanation: A small but effective opener. Hank's eagerness to be funny before the show even starts is perfectly in character — he's desperate to matter. The self-undermining joke sets his tone efficiently.

dialogue.speaker: Warm-up Comedian
dialogue.line: Apple sauce. No, no, I'm kidding. It says applause.

jokes.text: The announcer introduces Larry with: 'And now because he needs you more than you need him, larryyyyyy... Sanders!'
jokes.setup: Standard late-night show intro formula building Larry up
jokes.punchline: 'Because he needs you more than you need him' — subverts the hype by exposing Larry's emotional dependency on audience approval, which is the show's central thesis
jokes.explanation: Brilliant economy. The standard late-night announcer intro is inverted to reveal the show's core satirical premise — Larry is emotionally needy — in six words. It functions as both a joke and a mission statement for the entire series. High craft.

dialogue.line: And now because he needs you more than you need him, larryyyyyy... Sanders!

jokes.text: Larry complimenting the crowd: 'You are an exceptionally hot crowd for the middle of the week.'
jokes.setup: Larry thanks the audience effusively with mounting qualifications
jokes.punchline: 'For the middle of the week' — the compliment self-destructs mid-sentence; the qualifier reveals it's actually a lukewarm endorsement
jokes.explanation: Classic Larry passive-aggression dressed as warmth. The joke hinges on the rhythm of his praise collapsing at the last moment. The stalling repetition of 'may I say this' before the reveal is well-structured.

dialogue.speaker: Larry
dialogue.line: you are an exceptionally hot crowd for the middle of the week.

jokes.text: Monologue joke: Tom Arnold and Roseanne split up — 'to prove that his career is not in trouble, Tom was recently seen dating Tim Allen.'
jokes.setup: Tom and Roseanne's split, framed as Tom needing to prove career is fine
jokes.punchline: Dating Tim Allen — the joke implies both men's careers are equally in trouble, or satirizes the absurdity of celebrity damage control
jokes.explanation: Functional topical monologue joke. The punchline works on two levels (gay subtext + career mockery) but feels like standard late-night fodder of the era. Competent, not inspired.

dialogue.line: America's favorite couple, Tom and roseanne, have split up, but to prove that his career is not in trouble, Tom was recently seen dating tim allen.

jokes.text: College stats joke: 76% of seniors are sexually active vs. 50% of freshmen, therefore 'Stay in school.'
jokes.setup: Citing a study about college students' sexual activity rates by year
jokes.punchline: 'Stay in school. You may yet get laid.' — inverts the public service message into a purely carnal motivation
jokes.explanation: Well-structured two-step joke. The setup is legitimately informative, the first punchline lands, and then the second beat ('Only I, Larry Sanders, can say...') adds a meta layer of Larry's self-importance that elevates it beyond standard monologue.

dialogue.speaker: Larry
dialogue.line: 76% of college seniors are sexually active, but only 50% of college freshmen are. So I have one message to all of you young people out there... stay in school.

jokes.text: 'You see the athletes preach that. You see the politician preach that. But only I, Larry Sanders, can say, Stay in school. You may yet get laid.'
jokes.setup: The standard 'stay in school' public service message delivered by celebrities
jokes.punchline: Larry's narcissistic claim that only HE can uniquely deliver this sex-based spin on the message — exposing his grandiosity
jokes.explanation: The extension of the previous joke is where the real character comedy lives. Larry claiming a unique franchise on lewdness-as-advice is beautifully specific to his character. Strong character integration.

dialogue.speaker: Larry
dialogue.line: You see the athletes preach that. You see the politician preach that. But only I, Larry Sanders, can say, 'stay in school. You may yet get laid.'

jokes.text: 'Add to tonight's show a rudder and a sail, and it would have won America's Cup.' — Larry's post-monologue self-assessment
jokes.setup: Coming back from commercial, Larry makes a show of praising the lineup
jokes.punchline: Bizarre nautical metaphor for show quality that makes no logical sense but is delivered with complete confidence
jokes.explanation: Larry's absurd confidence in a non-sequitur compliment is very Shandling. The joke is in his complete commitment to a metaphor that doesn't hold up to scrutiny — perfect for the character.

dialogue.speaker: Larry
dialogue.line: Add to tonight's show a rudder and a sail, and it would have won America's cup.

dialogue.speaker: Larry
dialogue.line: What is wrong with you?

dialogue.speaker: Hank
dialogue.line: I thought it was more like the indy 500.

jokes.text: Larry asks Beverly to call Jason Alexander about Laker tickets but 'Don't let him know that I'm asking about it.'
jokes.setup: Larry wants floor seats from Jason Alexander but is too proud to ask directly
jokes.punchline: The comical indirectness — asking his assistant to secretly inquire — reveals Larry's social insecurity disguised as casualness
jokes.explanation: This is quintessential Larry — can't ask for things directly, needs a buffer for every social interaction. The comedy is in the transparent neediness wrapped in practiced nonchalance.

dialogue.speaker: Hank
dialogue.line: No, there was 3 points from outside! Swish! Nothing but net.

jokes.text: Larry can't remember the song he wants, tells Beverly to ask the Tower Records guy — then tries to sing it: '♪ dum dum dum ♪ ♪ nuum nuuum ♪'
jokes.setup: Larry wants a song from Tower Records but can't name it or the artist
jokes.punchline: He hums an incomprehensible approximation and asks Beverly to sing it to the Tower Records employee on the phone
jokes.explanation: The visual/audio absurdity of Larry's nonsense humming is perfectly executed, and the escalation to 'you sing it to him' nails the punchline. Efficient and character-true — Larry expects Beverly to solve impossible tasks.

dialogue.speaker: Larry
dialogue.line: Call Jason Alexander, and ask him if the... would you hold for a moment? Would you ask him if the laker tickets he has are floor seats? And don't let him know that I'm asking about it.

jokes.text: Artie finds a prescription in Larry's ATM receipts labeled 'Rectumin' — 'What is this? Rectumin.' 'That sounds familiar. What's that for?' 'For what it sounds like.' 'That is for nasal congestion.'
jokes.setup: Artie is sorting through Larry's ATM receipts and finds a prescription
jokes.punchline: The drug name sounds like 'rectum' — the answer 'for what it sounds like' followed by 'nasal congestion' is a double misdirection
jokes.explanation: A beautifully constructed three-beat joke. Beat 1: 'Rectumin' (audience thinks it's a butt drug). Beat 2: 'For what it sounds like' (confirms butt). Beat 3: 'That is for nasal congestion' (total reversal). The structure is unusually tight for this type of show.

dialogue.speaker: Beverly
dialogue.line: He said it would help if you knew the name of the song or the artist.

dialogue.speaker: Larry
dialogue.line: I just can't get it. I heard it on the radio.

dialogue.speaker: Beverly
dialogue.line: Well, sing it.

dialogue.speaker: Larry
dialogue.line: It's a woman... ♪ dum dum dum ♪ ♪ nuum nuuum ♪

dialogue.speaker: Beverly
dialogue.line: you sing it to him.

jokes.text: Artie: 'So... technically, your account is a big slush fund for the entire Pacific Rim.'
jokes.setup: Larry lists everyone with access to his ATM: business manager, assistant, agent, gardener, housekeeper
jokes.punchline: Artie's deadpan summation — 'slush fund for the entire Pacific Rim' — reframes Larry's careless trust as geopolitical absurdity
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's best lines. Artie's ability to reduce Larry's paranoid chaos to a single devastating summary is the essence of his character. 'Pacific Rim' is the perfect escalating word choice — it could have been 'everyone' but instead it lands as geopolitical satire of LA celebrity culture. Highly quotable, exceptional economy, perfect character voice.

dialogue.speaker: Larry
dialogue.line: Someone is stealing money from my atm account. You got a doctor's prescription mixed up in here. What is this? 'Rectumin.' That sounds familiar. What's that for?

dialogue.speaker: Artie
dialogue.line: For what it sounds like.

dialogue.speaker: Larry
dialogue.line: That is for nasal congestion.

jokes.text: Artie's follow-up: 'Just how bad is the nasal congestion?' — returning to the Rectumin bit after the ATM crisis
jokes.setup: The conversation has moved on from the Rectumin prescription to the ATM theft crisis
jokes.punchline: Artie circles back to asking about Larry's nasal congestion — implying he's prioritizing the bodily detail over the financial crisis
jokes.explanation: A well-executed callback that rewards attention. Artie's deliberate return to the medical detail in the middle of a financial scandal is funny because of what it implies about his priorities — or his desire to deflect Larry's anxiety.

dialogue.speaker: Larry
dialogue.line: Who has access to your atm account? My business manager. And his assistant. My agent. Gardener and housekeeper.

dialogue.speaker: Artie
dialogue.line: So... technically, your account is a big slush fund for the entire pacific rim.

jokes.text: Jason Alexander's Lakers tickets turn out to be 'loge' seats. Larry's reaction: 'The loge?' — repeated three times — then has Beverly cancel with an excuse.
jokes.setup: Larry had Beverly secretly inquire about Jason Alexander's Laker tickets, hoping for floor seats
jokes.punchline: They're loge — and Larry can't hide his horror; 'The loge?' repeated with escalating disbelief is his entire emotional response before coldly canceling
jokes.explanation: The repetition of 'the loge' is the joke — Larry's snobbery about seating conveyed entirely through vocal emphasis and the clinical manner in which he instructs Beverly to cancel. Character comedy at its most efficient.

dialogue.speaker: Beverly
dialogue.line: Jason Alexander's seats are in the loge.

dialogue.speaker: Larry
dialogue.line: The loge?

dialogue.speaker: Beverly
dialogue.line: Yes.

dialogue.speaker: Larry
dialogue.line: In the loge.

dialogue.speaker: Beverly
dialogue.line: In the loge?

dialogue.speaker: Larry
dialogue.line: The loge.

jokes.text: The tie color argument: Larry insists he said 'plum,' Beverly says he said 'peach.' Larry concedes 'maybe you said plum, but you said peach.'
jokes.setup: Pastel ties are delivered and Larry doesn't like them; a he-said/she-said begins
jokes.punchline: Larry's grammatically contradictory capitulation — 'maybe you said plum, but YOU said peach' — is logically nonsensical but delivered with full conviction
jokes.explanation: The logical paradox in Larry's line ('maybe you said plum, but you said peach' — both 'you') is either a brilliant slip or intentional. Either way, it perfectly captures Larry refusing to concede while appearing to concede. Cringe-funny because Beverly has to absorb this.

dialogue.speaker: Larry
dialogue.line: Call him and tell him that... that you're busy tomorrow night but thank you anyway.

jokes.text: Beverly delivers mail and 'your ointment.' Larry: 'Tennis elbow. This is my tennis elbow ointment, right? Yes. Good. I wasn't gonna ask.'
jokes.setup: Beverly hands Larry an ointment while others are present
jokes.punchline: 'I wasn't gonna ask.' — Larry's preemptive self-justification reveals he WAS about to ask and is embarrassed about it
jokes.explanation: Understated character comedy. Larry's need to confirm the ointment is for tennis elbow (not something embarrassing) while claiming he doesn't need confirmation is classic Shandling vanity.

dialogue.speaker: Larry
dialogue.line: These are too pastel-ish.

dialogue.speaker: Beverly
dialogue.line: Well, you're the one who said peach.

dialogue.speaker: Larry
dialogue.line: No, I said, uh, plum.

dialogue.speaker: Beverly
dialogue.line: No, you didn't say plum.

dialogue.speaker: Larry
dialogue.line: I said plum. I heard... OK. Well, maybe you said plum, but you said peach.

jokes.text: Larry won't talk to his father on the phone. Beverly urges him. Larry applies ointment and says: 'I'm getting relief already.'
jokes.setup: Beverly tells Larry he has to talk to his father; Larry is avoiding it
jokes.punchline: 'I'm getting relief already' — said while applying ointment, suggesting the ointment provides more comfort than family communication
jokes.explanation: The double meaning — physical relief from ointment vs. emotional avoidance — is beautifully compressed. Larry uses the literal to escape the figurative. Excellent economy with good character integration.

dialogue.speaker: Larry
dialogue.line: Tennis elbow. This is my tennis elbow ointment, right?

dialogue.speaker: Beverly
dialogue.line: Yes.

dialogue.speaker: Larry
dialogue.line: Good. I wasn't gonna ask.

jokes.text: Artie: 'Remind him to wipe the Rectumin from his elbow.' (about Larry going to dinner with Carrie Fisher)
jokes.setup: Larry is going out to dinner with Carrie Fisher tonight
jokes.punchline: Artie's callback to the nasal ointment being applied to the elbow — now framed as dating advice
jokes.explanation: A layered callback that consolidates two running threads (Rectumin + the ointment) into a single devastating joke delivered as offhand dating advice. Artie's deadpan makes it land harder. The Carrie Fisher name-drop adds the celebrity-world seasoning the show excels at.

dialogue.speaker: Beverly
dialogue.line: Oh, yeah, your father called. What does he want this time?

dialogue.speaker: Larry
dialogue.line: I don't know.

dialogue.speaker: Beverly
dialogue.line: Well, would you handle it for me?

dialogue.speaker: Beverly
dialogue.line: Larry, sooner or later you're gonna have to talk to the man.

dialogue.speaker: Larry
dialogue.line: No, I don't. I'm getting relief already.

jokes.text: Beverly keeps calling Larry to pick up for his father. He dodges repeatedly — walking past doors, ignoring the phone — as she escalates: 'Larry. Pick it up.' 'Don't go out that door, Larry.'
jokes.setup: Larry's father is on the phone; Larry refuses to engage
jokes.punchline: The sustained, escalating game of cat-and-mouse — Beverly's increasingly firm commands vs. Larry's increasingly creative avoidance — plays as physical comedy even though it's dialogue-driven
jokes.explanation: The comedy is in the sustained tension and Beverly's precise, increasingly weary escalation. 'Don't go out that door, Larry' is a line that only works because of what came before. Solid cringe-running gag structure.

dialogue.speaker: Beverly
dialogue.line: He's going out tonight, right?

dialogue.speaker: Artie
dialogue.line: Yeah.

dialogue.speaker: Beverly
dialogue.line: Dinner with Carrie Fisher.

dialogue.speaker: Artie
dialogue.line: Remind him to wipe the rectumin from his elbow.

jokes.text: Hank about his assistant: 'She's the best! I wouldn't know what to do if she left me. I couldn't brush my, uh... my teeth without her... literally.'
jokes.setup: Hank is praising his assistant to the visitor
jokes.punchline: 'Literally' — the hyperbole becomes uncomfortable reality; Hank may actually need someone to brush his teeth for him
jokes.explanation: The 'literally' lands because Tambor plays it with genuine uncertainty — it's unclear if it's hyperbole or a depressing truth. Either interpretation is funny.

dialogue.speaker: Hank
dialogue.line: You realize this is only the second time that you've paid us the honor of a visit. That doesn't seem possible. Is that right? It is, isn't it? Yeah. And I have the photo to prove it... july 12, 1991. I remember.

jokes.text: Hank's visitor abruptly asks: 'Do you have trouble trusting anybody who handles your finances?' — a non-sequitur that reveals he's there about the ATM theft
jokes.setup: The scene has been playing as a friendly visit; the visitor suddenly pivots
jokes.punchline: The abrupt topic shift to finances reveals the visit was investigative, not social — undercutting everything Hank just performed
jokes.explanation: The tonal whiplash is the joke — Hank's eager hospitality crashes against the visitor's blunt interrogation. The silence before the response would be palpable on screen.

dialogue.speaker: Hank
dialogue.line: I wouldn't know what to do if she left me. I couldn't brush my, uh... my teeth without her... literally.

jokes.text: Hank: 'You're having money problems, huh?' Visitor: 'No. Just some of the numbers don't add up right.' Hank: 'I don't need the details. Gimme the figure.' — then Hank reacts with 'Damn it.'
jokes.setup: The visitor is probing about money; Hank tries to play the big benefactor
jokes.punchline: 'Damn it.' — Hank's reaction to the $50,000 figure: he wanted to offer the money but clearly can't swing it
jokes.explanation: Hank's 'Damn it' is a perfect Tambor beat — the big gesture deflating instantly. The joke is in the gap between his performance of wealth and his actual financial reality. Strong character work.

dialogue.speaker: Hank
dialogue.line: You're having money problems, huh?

dialogue.speaker: Larry
dialogue.line: No. Just some of the numbers don't add up right.

dialogue.speaker: Hank
dialogue.line: I don't need the details. Gimme the figure.

dialogue.speaker: Hank
dialogue.line: Damn it.

jokes.text: Hank explains he can't lend $50,000: 'I'm having some plumbing problems down in the, uh... the Look Around Cafe...' — then: 'Just kidding. I don't need any money.'
jokes.setup: Hank is trying to explain why he can't provide the money while saving face
jokes.punchline: 'Just kidding. I don't need any money.' — The desperate pivot after using a random business as cover; the backtrack is more embarrassing than the original excuse
jokes.explanation: Hank's social panic — offering a plumbing excuse and then immediately killing the excuse — is perfectly cringe. 'Just kidding' as a financial retraction is inherently funny.

dialogue.speaker: Hank
dialogue.line: You know... I'd like to do this, but I'm having... it's a little hard for me to swing right now. I'll tell you why. I'm having some plumbing problems down in the, uh... the look around cafe... and, um... just kidding. I don't need any money.

jokes.text: Artie tells Beverly not to 'badger our Larry' — 'He's a grown man, sweetie. If he doesn't want to talk to his daddy, he doesn't have to.'
jokes.setup: Beverly is trying to get Larry to take his father's call
jokes.punchline: Artie's protective defense of Larry's right to ignore his own father, calling him 'our Larry' and 'sweetie' — treating it as a matter of sovereignty
jokes.explanation: Artie's paternalistic defense of Larry's childish behavior is funnier because Artie is simultaneously enabling and enabling with full awareness. 'Our Larry' treats the star like a species to be protected.

dialogue.speaker: Artie
dialogue.line: I hope you're not badgering our Larry. He's a grown man, sweetie. If he doesn't want to talk to his daddy, he doesn't have to.

dialogue.speaker: Beverly
dialogue.line: Do you think I enjoy chasing him down, Artie?

jokes.text: Beverly's workplace grievance list: scheduling, phone calls, family therapist, tie shopping, picking tomatoes out of his salad.
jokes.setup: Beverly vents about the scope of her job to Artie
jokes.punchline: The escalation from legitimate PA duties to 'pick the tomatoes out of his salad' — the list builds to an absurdly petty final item
jokes.explanation: The escalating absurdity of Beverly's job list works as both comedy and commentary on celebrity entitlement. 'Pick the tomatoes out of his salad' is the perfect terminal item — specific, domestic, utterly undignified for a PA.

dialogue.speaker: Beverly
dialogue.line: Well, when I came here, when I took this job, I came here under the assumption that I was to do his schedule and return his phone calls, not play family therapist and do his tie shopping and pick the tomatoes out of his salad.

jokes.text: Artie: 'Darling, the job is to keep our little host happy... whatever that takes.' Beverly: 'Well, sometimes I think it takes too much.' Artie: 'I thank you from the bottom of my heart for Larry's ma'am.'
jokes.setup: Beverly complains that Larry never says thank you; Artie says the job is to keep Larry happy
jokes.punchline: Artie thanking Beverly on Larry's behalf, in Larry's voice, with mock-formal sincerity — simultaneously validating her complaint and dismissing it
jokes.explanation: Artie performing proxy gratitude on Larry's behalf is a wonderfully compressed bit of character comedy. The 'ma'am' ending is oddly formal and perfect. It establishes the thank-you theme that pays off later in Beverly's arc.

dialogue.speaker: Beverly
dialogue.line: Darling, the job is to keep our little host happy... whatever that takes. Well, sometimes I think it takes too much. And do you think it would kill him if he could just say thank you just once?

dialogue.speaker: Artie
dialogue.line: I thank you from the bottom of my heart for Larry's ma'am.

jokes.text: Larry trying on the sketch costume, Beverly: 'I swear, if I looked any fatter...' Larry: 'Oh, knock it off. You look terrific.'
jokes.setup: Beverly sees herself in a mirror apparently while helping Larry
jokes.punchline: Larry's reflexive reassurance — delivered the same way he'd reassure a guest — is clearly performative rather than genuine
jokes.explanation: A light moment. Larry's automatic compliment dispensing is in character but the joke is understated and not particularly memorable.

dialogue.speaker: Hank
dialogue.line: I just kept calling you... Kramer out there. I'm... I'm sorry.

dialogue.speaker: Jason Alexander
dialogue.line: No, that's all right. It's an easy mistake. It's just that I love the show so much, and I just keep getting you and your character mixed up.

dialogue.speaker: Hank
dialogue.line: Yeah... ha ha ha. Well, th... that's weird, 'cause I... I play George on the show. Michael Richards plays Kramer.

jokes.text: Artie's emotional appeal to Larry about his estranged father: 'My father... left us. I never had the chance to say the things that I always wanted to say to him...' Larry: 'Listen... believe it or not, neither do I.'
jokes.setup: Artie delivers a sincere, moving speech about his own father dying before reconciliation
jokes.punchline: 'Believe it or not, neither do I.' — Larry agrees with the WRONG part of the argument; he doesn't want to say those things to his father either
jokes.explanation: This is the episode's finest joke. Artie delivers a genuinely touching speech — Rip Torn sells it completely — then Larry deflects with a line that is both hilarious and character-defining. The punchline works because it inverts the expected emotional response without being cynical — Larry's self-awareness about his own avoidance is honest AND funny. The 'believe it or not' prefix is perfect: he knows it's a bad answer. This is the kind of joke that makes Larry Sanders great television, not just a comedy. Exceptional character integration — no other character on any other show could deliver this line.

dialogue.speaker: Larry
dialogue.line: He could have been calling you Elaine. That's what he called tim allen last week.

jokes.text: Larry finally calls his father and immediately leads with: 'Did you get to see the show last night? We had Jonathan Winters on, and I know he's one of your favorites.'
jokes.setup: Larry has been guilted into calling his estranged father
jokes.punchline: His opening gambit is not a personal connection but a plug for his own show — the emotional reconciliation is immediately co-opted by his ego
jokes.explanation: The comedy is devastating in its specificity: Larry, forced into vulnerability, immediately retreats to his professional identity. The show-plug framed as father-son bonding is both funny and painful — perfectly Larry.

dialogue.speaker: Jason Alexander
dialogue.line: We had these crappy loge seats, and ovitz calls me, and he's giving us front row seats right next to nicholson.

dialogue.speaker: Larry
dialogue.line: Di-did you say Wednesday?

dialogue.speaker: Jason Alexander
dialogue.line: Really? No, no, it's Thursday.

dialogue.speaker: Larry
dialogue.line: Oh.

dialogue.speaker: Beverly
dialogue.line: You know what? You're free on Thursday.

dialogue.speaker: Jason Alexander
dialogue.line: Good.

dialogue.speaker: Larry
dialogue.line: Oh. I'm in.

jokes.text: Larry realizing his father hasn't seen ANY of his shows: 'Have you seen any of them? Yeah.'
jokes.setup: Larry is shocked his father didn't catch the Jonathan Winters episode
jokes.punchline: The pause before 'Yeah' from the father (implied) — then Larry's flat 'Yeah.' — the revelation that dad watches but never mentions it lands as both funny and sad
jokes.explanation: A quieter moment. Larry realizing his father does watch but never said so is a character beat delivered through silence and a deflated 'Yeah.' Functional but subtle.

dialogue.speaker: Artie
dialogue.line: What do you want me to do, take him to dinner, get him hammered, couple of hookers?

dialogue.speaker: Larry
dialogue.line: No, no. That would be overkill. Just be yourself.

jokes.text: Larry's father says he wants to visit — tomorrow. Larry's reaction: 'Tomorrow? Perfect. No, I look forward to that.' — then immediately pivots to logistics ('First class. Yes. And I'll have Beverly pick you up.')
jokes.setup: Larry has just had an emotional moment and his father asks to visit
jokes.punchline: 'Perfect.' — said with the exact tone of someone for whom this is deeply imperfect — followed by the mechanical logistics of someone managing an inconvenient situation
jokes.explanation: The speed with which Larry converts the emotional into the logistical is very funny. 'I'll have Beverly pick you up' immediately converts father-son warmth into task-delegation.

dialogue.speaker: Artie
dialogue.line: Hey, Jerry! How the hell are ya? It's always a delight to greet my second favorite Mr. Sanders.

jokes.text: Larry after hanging up: 'Beverly? Would you get the tape with the ocean sounds? My father's coming tomorrow. I'm gonna be lying facedown. Gimme some sand and some sea urchins. Damn it.'
jokes.setup: Larry just agreed to have his father visit; he now needs to process this
jokes.punchline: The escalating stress-response: ocean sounds → facedown → sand and sea urchins → 'Damn it' — each item more absurdly elaborate than the last
jokes.explanation: A beautifully constructed escalation. The requests build from reasonable (ambient sounds) to absurd (sea urchins) with perfect comedic rhythm. 'Gimme some sand and some sea urchins' is an extraordinary sentence — the specificity of sea urchins (not just 'sand and waves') is what makes it exceptional. High quotability, strong character voice.

dialogue.speaker: Larry's Father
dialogue.line: I guess beverly didn't know I prefer the window.

dialogue.speaker: Larry
dialogue.line: Yeah, well, that'll knock it out of you, dad.

jokes.text: Hank mistakes Jason Alexander for Kramer (Michael Richards' character). Jason corrects him: 'I play George on the show. Michael Richards plays Kramer.'
jokes.setup: Hank is enthusiastically greeting Jason Alexander backstage
jokes.punchline: Hank has been calling him 'Kramer' — wrong character, wrong actor — and Jason has to gently correct him
jokes.explanation: Hank calling Jason Alexander 'Kramer' is a perfect expression of his obliviousness and desperation to connect with celebrity. The meta-layer (Seinfeld actors on a rival late-night show, getting mixed up by the host's sidekick) gives it extra industry-satire punch.

dialogue.speaker: Larry
dialogue.line: When you got money from me the other day, you didn't give anybody my atm password, did you?

dialogue.speaker: Phil
dialogue.line: No, but you gotta admit that l-a-r-r-y is pretty easy to guess.

jokes.text: Larry apologizes to Jason for Hank's Kramer mix-up: 'He could have been calling you Elaine. That's what he called Tim Allen last week.'
jokes.setup: Larry is damage-controlling after Hank's Kramer mistake
jokes.punchline: The revelation that Hank called Tim Allen 'Elaine' last week — a female character applied to a male celebrity — is the escalating payoff
jokes.explanation: This is a superb callback escalation. The original mistake (wrong male character) is topped by a worse mistake (female character for a male guest). The specificity of 'Elaine' for 'Tim Allen' is perfect — it's not just wrong, it's wrong in the funniest possible direction. Highly quotable, exceptional economy.

dialogue.speaker: Phil
dialogue.line: What, to Sanders? Hardy-har-har.

jokes.text: Artie to Jason Alexander: 'My boy, when are they going to give you your own show?' — before disappearing
jokes.setup: Artie greets Jason Alexander warmly as he passes through
jokes.punchline: The question implies Jason Alexander should have his own show — which, given Seinfeld's success, is absurdly out of touch, OR is Artie being genuinely complimentary about George Costanza's specific appeal
jokes.explanation: The joke works on the meta level — Jason Alexander is already on the biggest show in America (Seinfeld), so the question is comically ignorant or a backhanded compliment. Artie's breezy disappearance after asking adds to the charm.

dialogue.speaker: Hank
dialogue.line: You're his sidekick?
Yes, sir. Second banana. You know, I like to think of myself as second in command.

dialogue.speaker: Larry's Father
dialogue.line: Here you go. Like Ed mcmahon.

dialogue.speaker: Hank
dialogue.line: Exactly like Ed mcmahon.

dialogue.speaker: Larry's Father
dialogue.line: That's a pretty sweet deal. Take home a big paycheck just for holding down a couch and selling crap.

jokes.text: The Laker ticket manipulation: Larry discovers Jason has been upgraded from loge to front row next to Nicholson — suddenly his schedule clears; Beverly desperately tries to cover: 'Oh. I'm sor... you're not free... he can't make it.'
jokes.setup: Larry had Beverly cancel the laker game because seats were in the loge; now Jason reveals front-row seats next to Nicholson
jokes.punchline: Larry's immediate reversal ('Di-did you say Wednesday? Really?') while Beverly frantically tries to maintain the lie they've already told
jokes.explanation: The payoff on the loge setup is excellent. Larry's transparent reversal ('Di-did you say Wednesday?') combined with Beverly's panicked damage control creates perfectly calibrated cringe. The three-way dynamic — Larry trying to reinstate himself, Beverly trying to maintain the lie, Jason oblivious — is masterfully orchestrated.

dialogue.speaker: Hank
dialogue.line: You know, for just a split second there, you reminded me of the old man himself. Henry Joseph Kingsley.

jokes.text: Jason to Larry: 'Hey, listen, Jerry says you're doing great. The monologues are really getting funny now.'
jokes.setup: Jason is making small talk before leaving
jokes.punchline: 'Really getting funny now' implies they weren't before — a backhanded compliment from a peer, referencing 'Jerry' (Seinfeld) as an authority on Larry's comedy
jokes.explanation: A perfectly calibrated Hollywood insult disguised as a compliment. 'Really getting funny now' is the stinger — it damns with faint praise in a way only a peer could deliver. The casual 'Jerry says' name-drop is an additional layer of Hollywood social currency being exchanged.

dialogue.speaker: Artie
dialogue.line: Beverly, I thank you from the bottom of my heart for handing Larry his undies. Larry thanks you, too. Don't you?

jokes.text: Larry asking Artie to help with his father: 'What do you want me to do, take him to dinner, get him hammered, couple of hookers?' Larry: 'No, no. That would be overkill. Just be yourself.'
jokes.setup: Larry is anxious about his father's visit and asks Artie for help managing him
jokes.punchline: 'That would be overkill' — Larry's only objection to the hookers plan is that it's excessive; 'just be yourself' implies Artie being himself is already halfway there
jokes.explanation: The joke operates on multiple levels: Artie's casually transgressive list, Larry's non-objection to the substance of it ('that would be overkill' accepts the premise), and 'just be yourself' as a punchline that implies Artie's natural personality is already entertainment enough. Efficient and character-true.

dialogue.speaker: Hank
dialogue.line: Your father's a big pain in the ass.

jokes.text: Larry's father Jerry arrives and complains about having an aisle seat on the plane: 'I had an aisle seat. I guess Beverly didn't know I prefer the window.' Larry: 'Yeah, well, that'll knock it out of you, dad.'
jokes.setup: Father has flown first class at Larry's expense and arrives exhausted
jokes.punchline: The complaint is an aisle seat, not a window — completely petty given that he's on a first-class ticket — and Larry's sarcastic validation ('that'll knock it out of you') acknowledges the absurdity without calling it out
jokes.explanation: The mirroring of Larry's ingratitude with his father's ingratitude is the episode's central theme crystallized in a joke. Jerry complaining about an aisle seat on a first-class ticket he was given for free immediately tells us everything about the Sanders father-son dynamic.

dialogue.speaker: Larry
dialogue.line: I hate to agree with Hank, but I guess it's so. No matter what you do for my dad, I swear to God, there's never a thank you, like that would kill him.

jokes.text: Larry's father says he didn't come for fun: 'I just had to get away from Karen for a while. We've been arguing again.'
jokes.setup: Artie cheerfully asks what the boys are going to do for fun
jokes.punchline: The father reveals he's not here for father-son bonding at all — he's fleeing his wife — deflating the emotional setup entirely
jokes.explanation: The reveal is perfectly timed and darkly funny — Larry's father visiting is not about Larry at all. It extends the father-son mirror: Larry uses people without acknowledgment; his father does the same to Larry.

dialogue.speaker: Beverly
dialogue.line: All I know is it's the most frustrating thing in the world trying to please someone who doesn't appreciate anything you do.

dialogue.speaker: Larry
dialogue.line: That is exactly right.

jokes.text: 'Post show critique.' / 'What?' / 'Post show critique.' / 'Gotcha. Sure. Right away.' — Artie inventing a fake meeting to rescue Larry
jokes.setup: Larry needs an escape from his father mid-conversation; Artie appears in the doorway
jokes.punchline: Artie invents an institutional-sounding excuse ('post show critique') — Larry plays along immediately — the code-switching is completely transparent but nobody acknowledges it
jokes.explanation: The double exchange of 'post show critique' is perfectly executed. Artie's deadpan invention of bureaucracy as an escape hatch, Larry's immediate synchronization, and the father left alone in the room is all delivered in seconds. Artie as Larry's enabler is the show's great secondary dynamic.

dialogue.speaker: Beverly
dialogue.line: I know who stole your money.

jokes.text: Artie compliments Larry's tie — 'Nice tie, by the way.' — which is one of the contested peach/plum ties from earlier. Larry says 'Just something I picked up.' Artie: 'Yeah. It looks familiar.'
jokes.setup: Earlier there was a whole argument about peach vs. plum ties being 'too pastel'
jokes.punchline: Artie's 'It looks familiar' — a knowing acknowledgment that this is the tie Larry was complaining about; Larry's denial ('just something I picked up') is self-incriminating
jokes.explanation: A beautifully quiet callback. Artie sees through Larry's pretense instantly ('it looks familiar') and says nothing more. The economy is exceptional — three words do all the work. Rewards attentive viewers.

dialogue.speaker: Beverly
dialogue.line: I know. I took it.

dialogue.speaker: Larry
dialogue.line: You took it.

dialogue.speaker: Beverly
dialogue.line: Yes, I took it. If you wanted to know why, why didn't you ask me, and I would have told you.

jokes.text: Phil and Larry on the ATM password: 'You didn't give anybody my ATM password, did you?' Phil: 'No, but you gotta admit that L-A-R-R-Y is pretty easy to guess.' Larry: 'Yeah. I changed that.' Phil: 'You changed it? What, to Sanders?'
jokes.setup: Larry asks if Phil gave out his ATM password
jokes.punchline: His password was literally his own first name; Phil guesses the obvious upgrade would be his last name
jokes.explanation: Solid joke. Larry's password being 'LARRY' is the perfect expression of his narcissistic obliviousness to security. Phil's 'Hardy-har-har... What, to Sanders?' is a good escalation — and pays off at the end of the episode with 'Leno.'

dialogue.speaker: Beverly
dialogue.line: Because 3 months ago, you had me drive to encino looking for a paint chip from your decorator. I spent 3 hours in traffic, Larry. That's 3 hours for a paint chip, so I charged you.

jokes.text: Beverly's grievance speech interrupted by Larry: 'Listen. We have to change my ATM password, Beverly.' Beverly: 'Why?' 'Phil guessed it.' Beverly: 'And this is your son.' 'This is Billy Crystal.'
jokes.setup: Beverly is in the middle of an emotional grievance; Larry pivots to the ATM password
jokes.punchline: 'This is Billy Crystal.' — Larry handing Beverly what is clearly a photo of himself, claiming it's Billy Crystal, in the middle of an emotional conversation — a total non-sequitur deflection
jokes.explanation: The mid-emotional-crisis ATM pivot is funny enough, but 'This is Billy Crystal' as a subject change is delightfully absurd. The implication (Larry handing Beverly a photo he needs her to identify) adds another layer of demanding behavior mid-confrontation.

dialogue.speaker: Beverly
dialogue.line: It was on a Sunday, Larry! Yeah? So I charged you. And I charged you when you had me driving all over Los Angeles looking for peach-colored ties for you.

jokes.text: Artie showing Larry's father the show tapes: 'I only wish my dad could have seen my work. But by the time I got my first big boat show, he was, um...' — trails off with implication of death
jokes.setup: Artie is trying to impress upon Jerry Sanders how important it is to support his son's career
jokes.punchline: 'My first big boat show' — Artie's father dying before seeing his boat show is absurdly specific and undercuts the pathos
jokes.explanation: 'My first big boat show' is a genuinely funny specific choice — Artie's career is never quite what you expect, and the comedy is in the word 'boat.' The trailing off into implied death after 'boat show' creates an absurdly bathos-rich moment.

dialogue.speaker: Beverly
dialogue.line: And I charge you for picking up your frozen yogurt at 7 every morning so that you can have the first batch out of the machine. Every morning?

jokes.text: Jerry Sanders discovers Hank is the sidekick: 'You're his sidekick?' Hank: 'Yes, sir. Second banana.' / 'You know, I like to think of myself as second in command.' Jerry: 'Here you go. Like Ed McMahon.' Hank: 'Exactly like Ed McMahon.' Jerry: 'That's a pretty sweet deal. Take home a big paycheck just for holding down a couch and selling crap.'
jokes.setup: Hank is trying to present himself with dignity to Larry's father
jokes.punchline: Jerry's assessment of the Ed McMahon role — 'holding down a couch and selling crap' — is brutally accurate and delivered without malice, which makes it worse
jokes.explanation: Jerry unknowingly demolishes Hank's self-image in one sentence. 'Holding down a couch and selling crap' is an unusually accurate and devastating description of the second-banana role. Hank's 'Exactly like Ed McMahon' acceptance of the comparison — followed by the rug-pull — is beautifully played. High quotability.

dialogue.speaker: Beverly
dialogue.line: I'm tired of cleaning your ointment applicators.

jokes.text: Hank: 'You know, for just a split second there, you reminded me of the old man himself. Henry Joseph Kingsley.' — Beat — Jerry asks for a Classic Coke when he ordered Diet.
jokes.setup: Hank has had an emotional moment comparing Jerry to his own father
jokes.punchline: Jerry immediately undercuts the emotional beat by complaining about his drink order — mirroring Larry's father-son ingratitude theme
jokes.explanation: The emotional moment deflated by a petty drink complaint is a well-worn structure, but in context it reinforces the episode's theme about ingratitude and mirrors the Larry-Jerry dynamic. Hank's vulnerability immediately punished by reality is true to the show.

dialogue.speaker: Beverly
dialogue.line: I am tired of begging your father to come see the show so that you can feel good about yourself. Did you ask my dad to come and see the show?

jokes.text: Beverly is asked to hand Larry 'that pair of underwear over there' — and then asked to order more ('half this color, half black') — during a work meeting
jokes.setup: Beverly is in Larry's dressing room during a normal work interaction
jokes.punchline: Larry casually asking her to handle his underwear — and immediately treat it as a procurement task — is the ultimate expression of boundary-free celebrity entitlement
jokes.explanation: A perfect micro-example of the show's central satire: celebrity entitlement bleeding into the mundanely personal. Asking your PA to handle your underwear and immediately pivot to ordering more is both funny and a little disgusting.

dialogue.line: disgruntled postal workers say they need the extra revenue because of the rising cost of ammunition.

jokes.text: Artie: 'I thank you from the bottom of my heart for handing Larry his undies. Larry thanks you, too. Don't you?' Larry: 'Artie, please.'
jokes.setup: Earlier, Artie thanked Beverly on Larry's behalf for his PA duties
jokes.punchline: Artie repeats the proxy thank-you specifically for 'handing Larry his undies' — the callback is more absurd because the act being thanked is more demeaning
jokes.explanation: The callback to Artie's earlier proxy-gratitude bit, now applied to underwear-handling, is funnier than the original because of escalation. 'Larry thanks you, too. Don't you?' with Larry's mortified 'Artie, please' is a perfect button.

dialogue.speaker: Artie
dialogue.line: Well, if I spent 30 years selling office equipment, I'd be bitter about damn near everything.

jokes.text: Artie: 'Beverly, do me a favor and get Larry's father the hell out of my office.'
jokes.setup: The scene has been building tension around managing Jerry Sanders
jokes.punchline: Artie's blunt, profane order to remove Larry's father from the office — delivered as a casual aside — is the most direct thing anyone has said about the situation
jokes.explanation: Artie's directness is always funnier than the euphemisms around him. 'Get Larry's father the hell out of my office' in Rip Torn's voice is a reliable laugh — the casual profanity of a veteran showbiz operator.

dialogue.speaker: Larry
dialogue.line: This was returned by sinead o'Connor, sent back, uh... pasta sent back because there was a hair in it. Sinead o'Connor. There was a hair in it.

jokes.text: Beverly: 'All I know is it's the most frustrating thing in the world trying to please someone who doesn't appreciate anything you do.' Larry: 'That is exactly right.' — completely unaware she's talking about him
jokes.setup: Beverly appears to be reflecting on Larry's difficult relationship with his father
jokes.punchline: Larry enthusiastically agrees with her description of his father — which is a perfect description of Larry himself — without any self-awareness
jokes.explanation: This is the episode's other great joke, and its thematic heart. Beverly's observation is simultaneously about Larry's father AND Larry himself — the irony is perfect because it's been the episode's central argument. Larry's enthusiastic 'That is exactly right' without any self-recognition is devastating. The character integration is as high as it gets — this only works because we know Larry so well. A masterclass in dramatic irony used for comedy.

dialogue.speaker: Larry
dialogue.line: everything I got comedy-wise I owe to you. You're a terrific man, and I love you very much.

jokes.text: Beverly confesses she took $1,500 from Larry's ATM, and enumerates the charges: driving to Encino for a paint chip on a Sunday, peach-colored ties, frozen yogurt at 7am ('the first batch out of the machine'), cleaning ointment applicators
jokes.setup: Larry demands to know who stole from his ATM account
jokes.punchline: Beverly's list of charges is an escalating catalog of indignities — each item revealing a more absurd dimension of Larry's demands — ending with 'cleaning your ointment applicators'
jokes.explanation: A masterfully constructed escalation that serves as the episode's dramatic climax. Each item is funnier than the last — paint chip on a Sunday, peach ties, first-batch frozen yogurt at 7am, ointment applicators — and each one is a callback to something established earlier. The comedy and the drama are inseparable here, which is the show's great achievement. 'Cleaning your ointment applicators' as a terminal item is perfect.

dialogue.speaker: Larry
dialogue.line: and just say to my... assistant beverly, who I know is watching... I hope is watching... is probably not watching... but thank you, beverly, for everything you've done. I appreciate it, and thank you very much.

jokes.text: Beverly: 'I am tired of begging your father to come see the show so that you can feel good about yourself.' Larry: 'Did you ask my dad to come and see the show? What did he say?'
jokes.setup: Beverly is mid-breakdown about being taken for granted
jokes.punchline: Larry's ONLY response to Beverly's emotional revelation is curiosity about what his dad said — complete emotional obliviousness executed with perfect comedy timing
jokes.explanation: Larry's response is both hilarious and the most revealing moment in the episode. Beverly has just confessed to years of emotional labor and ATM theft in the name of her job — and Larry's first instinct is to ask what his dad said about the show. The character integration is perfect. This is what makes the show great: comedy that is also devastating character truth.

dialogue.speaker: Larry
dialogue.line: This is a plate licked clean by roseanne.

jokes.text: Beverly: 'Forget it, OK? Forget it.' Larry: 'Well, what is it? You want a raise? Is that it?' / 'This is not about money.' 'Well, if there's some job you're not comfortable doing, just ask the weird intern to do it.'
jokes.setup: Beverly is trying to articulate a genuine emotional grievance
jokes.punchline: 'Just ask the weird intern to do it.' — Larry reduces an emotional crisis to a task-management issue; the intern being 'weird' is a perfect throwaway detail
jokes.explanation: The 'weird intern' is a perfect detail — Larry knows the intern is 'weird' but doesn't know Beverly's emotional state. The joke is in his complete category error: treating a human crisis as a staffing issue.

dialogue.speaker: Artie
dialogue.line: He loved it. But he left.

dialogue.speaker: Larry
dialogue.line: You're kidding.

dialogue.speaker: Artie
dialogue.line: He had to catch an early plane to pittsburgh. He sends his love. Left right after the marilu henner segment.

jokes.text: Monologue joke: Disgruntled postal workers want a 3-cent stamp increase 'because of the rising cost of ammunition.'
jokes.setup: Postal workers need revenue for a stamp increase
jokes.punchline: 'Rising cost of ammunition' — referencing the 'going postal' cultural phenomenon of the early '90s
jokes.explanation: A dark topical joke that's efficient and lands. The 'going postal' joke was already becoming a standard trope by 1993, so originality is limited, but the specific framing ('rising cost of ammunition') is crisper than most versions of this joke.

dialogue.speaker: Jason Alexander
dialogue.line: Steve called, and he can't go. He's sick. So I asked Julia roberts to come along. Boing! Rah! See ya, kid.

jokes.text: Hank spots Larry's father in the audience: 'You gotta admit, there was definite negative vibe out there. That's why your monologue went right in the dumper.'
jokes.setup: Artie and Larry spot Jerry Sanders sitting in the audience
jokes.punchline: Hank immediately blames the father's presence for the bad monologue — exploiting any opportunity to critique Larry's performance
jokes.explanation: Hank's gleeful attribution of Larry's failure to the father is typically Hank — finding opportunity in Larry's discomfort. 'Right in the dumper' is a good specific phrase.

dialogue.speaker: Larry
dialogue.line: I wanted blueberry, and, uh, there's no pecans... but thanks.

jokes.text: Larry: 'Do you know this is the first time he's ever come to see me perform?' Hank: 'You're kidding.' Larry: 'He never thought I would make it. Now he's just been bitter.' Artie: 'Well, if I spent 30 years selling office equipment, I'd be bitter about damn near everything.'
jokes.setup: Larry is having an emotional moment about his father finally attending the show
jokes.punchline: Artie's matter-of-fact explanation for the father's bitterness — 30 years in office equipment sales — delivered without irony as the complete, sufficient explanation
jokes.explanation: Artie's line is exceptional. 'If I spent 30 years selling office equipment, I'd be bitter about damn near everything' is both a joke and a genuinely compassionate act of explanation. Rip Torn's delivery would make this land as one of the episode's big laughs. The specificity of 'office equipment' and 'damn near everything' is textbook Artie — world-weary but not cruel.

dialogue.speaker: Paula
dialogue.line: It's Leno now, right?

jokes.text: Phil brings Larry's 'butt cream' during the show: 'Um... Larry, here's your butt cream, and Beverly said that you might want some yogurt for after the show?' 'We're in the middle of the show right now.' 'Raspberry, OK? I'm...' 'Any toppings?' 'Would you please? Pecans.'
jokes.setup: Larry is in the middle of taping the show when Phil appears backstage
jokes.punchline: Larry's mortification at the butt cream delivery is immediately overcome by his engagement with yogurt toppings — pecans — mid-show
jokes.explanation: The escalation from butt cream embarrassment to pecan preferences mid-broadcast is perfectly Larry — his dignity outrage is always brief and always overtaken by his creature comforts. The 'what is that?' pause before 'poison oak' adds a solid extra beat.

jokes.text: The 'Food Sent Back by Famous Stars' sketch: Sinead O'Connor sent back pasta because 'there was a hair in it.'
jokes.setup: A recurring sketch about celebrity finicky dining
jokes.punchline: Sinead O'Connor — famously bald — sent back food because of a hair in it. The joke writes itself, and is left implicit.
jokes.explanation: The joke is almost entirely visual and implicit — Sinead O'Connor is bald, a hair in her food is impossible. The writers trust the audience to complete the joke. The restraint in not explaining it is the craft — this is how you write for smart viewers. Very high economy.

jokes.text: First food item: pasta returned by Sinead O'Connor because there was a hair in it. Larry and Hank let the irony hang in silence.
jokes.setup: The bit involves famous stars' returned food; first item is Sinead O'Connor's pasta
jokes.punchline: The joke is that Sinead O'Connor, famously bald, returned pasta for having a hair in it — the visual of a bald woman complaining about hair is the complete joke
jokes.explanation: A genuinely clever celebrity joke — the specificity of a bald celebrity returning food for a hair is a great premise. The joke is implicit, landing from the audience's recognition without needing to be explained. Strong structure and economy. One of the better on-air bits.

jokes.text: Larry introduces his father from the stage: 'Dad, stand up in the audience and say hello...' — then delivers a genuine, heartfelt tribute: 'Everything I got comedy-wise I owe to you.'
jokes.setup: Larry interrupts the sketch to publicly acknowledge his father
jokes.punchline: The tribute is sincere — but the comedy is in Larry using a nationally broadcast show as the vehicle for a private emotional reconciliation he couldn't achieve face-to-face
jokes.explanation: Larry can't say personal things in private but can broadcast them to millions. The comedy is bittersweet — it IS a genuine gesture, but its public nature is a Larry defense mechanism. Strong character integration.

jokes.text: Hank immediately hijacks Larry's father tribute to mention his own mother: 'You just reminded me of my mother who is watching tonight...' Larry: 'Hank, Hank, let's go on with the...'
jokes.setup: Larry is having a rare genuine public moment acknowledging his father
jokes.punchline: Hank pivots to his own mother within seconds — making the moment about himself — which is perfectly Hank
jokes.explanation: Perfectly character-true for Hank. Any emotional spotlight on Larry must be redirected to Hank within 10 seconds. The speed of the hijack and Larry's weary 'Hank, Hank' make it a reliable laugh.

jokes.text: Hank immediately hijacks Larry's father tribute to mention his own mother watching at home
jokes.setup: Larry has just done a sincere tribute to his father
jokes.punchline: Hank immediately inserts himself: 'You just reminded me of my mother who is watching tonight... well, that's all right. I wanna say mom...' — Larry has to cut him off
jokes.explanation: Classic Hank — he cannot resist centering himself at someone else's sincere moment. The comedy is in the absolute predictability of it and the zero self-awareness.

jokes.text: Larry extends the tribute to Beverly — 'I hope is watching... is probably not watching' — then Hank starts naming someone else: 'There's a young lady named Darlene...' Artie: 'Well, F me!'
jokes.setup: Larry tries to extend his public thanks to Beverly; Hank keeps trying to name people
jokes.punchline: Artie's explosive 'Well, F me!' — the profanity-as-punctuation to the now-out-of-control acknowledgment sequence — is the perfect button
jokes.explanation: Artie's outburst is the episode's most purely funny in-the-moment reaction. The escalation — from sincere tribute to Beverly to Hank hijacking to Artie's explosive frustration — is perfectly paced. 'Well, F me!' as the release valve on the whole sequence is exceptional. Rip Torn would absolutely destroy this line. High quotability, exceptional economy.

jokes.text: Larry struggles to open the last covered dish for 5 minutes on camera — 'The prop department... yes? No? This one I really want to get open' — building absurd anticipation
jokes.setup: The food sketch requires opening increasingly dramatic covered dishes
jokes.punchline: Larry spends an extended, uncomfortable time unable to open the final prop — 'You don't want to open... the prop department...' — the failure becomes the comedy
jokes.explanation: The comedy of anticipation and failure works well in performance — the live audience tension of watching someone struggle with a prop. On paper it loses some punch, but the length of the bit and Larry's commentary ('you hope that when you do a bit like this that something comes out...') is self-aware meta-comedy.

jokes.text: 'This, of course, was sent back... this is a plate licked clean by Roseanne.'
jokes.setup: The elaborate dish-opening sequence has been building to the final reveal
jokes.punchline: A plate licked clean — returned not because of a problem but because Roseanne ate everything — a fat joke and celebrity-meanness joke in one
jokes.explanation: The payoff to the long opening sequence earns some points for structure, and the callback to Roseanne from the monologue is neat. But the underlying joke is a celebrity fat joke — the lowest tier of easy comedy, even for 1993. The craft in the surrounding packaging is better than the joke itself.

jokes.text: After the emotional climax: Larry's father 'loved it' — but left immediately after the Marilu Henner segment. Larry: 'Well, that segment dragged anyway, didn't it?'
jokes.setup: Larry is told his father loved the show and asks where he is
jokes.punchline: Dad left after the Marilu Henner segment — and Larry's response is to critique that segment rather than process his father's absence
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's great endings. Larry hears his father left before he could see him and responds by critiquing the segment his dad left on. The self-protection is complete and heartbreaking — but the joke lands perfectly. 'That segment dragged anyway, didn't it?' is a beautifully sad-funny line. Very high character integration. The joke and the theme are one.

jokes.text: Artie: 'For what you did for your father tonight, I salute you. You're finally turning into the man I always thought you were.'
jokes.setup: Larry has just done the father tribute on live TV
jokes.punchline: 'You're finally turning into the man I always thought you were' — Artie's praise is genuinely moving, but the 'finally' is a quietly devastating qualifier
jokes.explanation: A great Artie line. The 'finally' is the tell — Artie has been waiting a long time for Larry to be the man he should be. It's warm and slightly damning simultaneously. Very Artie in its mixture of paternal pride and mild rebuke.

jokes.text: Larry: 'What you said about Beverly... hey, that was sweet.' Artie: 'Yeah. I don't do that often enough. Why is that? I wonder where the trait comes from?' Artie: 'Yeah!'
jokes.setup: Larry is reflecting warmly on his public thanks to Beverly
jokes.punchline: Artie's 'I wonder where the trait comes from?' — implying Larry inherited his ingratitude from his father — is delivered as a shared observation before Artie enthusiastically agrees with himself
jokes.explanation: Artie's final observation — 'I wonder where the trait comes from?' with his own enthusiastic 'Yeah!' — is the episode's thematic button, delivered as a gentle joke. He's connecting Larry's gratitude failure to his father's, and doing it while Larry completely misses the implication. Perfect character writing.

jokes.text: Jason Alexander reveals he's going to the Lakers game — with front-row seats — and Steve Guttenberg has been replaced by Julia Roberts. Artie: 'Boing! Rah! See ya, kid.'
jokes.setup: Larry realizes he's been bumped from the Lakers game he desperately wanted to attend
jokes.punchline: Artie's 'Boing! Rah!' — an ecstatic, cartoonish reaction to the Julia Roberts replacement — before immediately ditching Larry to join the group
jokes.explanation: Artie's 'Boing! Rah!' is a brilliantly specific piece of character comedy — Rip Torn's Artie expressing pure, unfiltered joy at the prospect of Julia Roberts, then immediately abandoning Larry without hesitation. 'See ya, kid' is the perfect cap. Larry is left alone with the consequences of his own social maneuvering.

jokes.text: Larry trying to send Beverly flowers — realizes he can't send flowers and can't ask her to send them to herself — asks Paula to do it, then offers his ATM card to pay.
jokes.setup: Larry wants to thank Beverly properly with flowers every Friday
jokes.punchline: The elaborate workaround needed for a simple gesture — because Larry is both incapable of sending flowers himself AND insane enough to consider asking her to send them to herself — is pure Larry
jokes.explanation: The comedy of Larry's incapacity to perform basic human gestures directly is well-established by this point. The beat where he genuinely considers asking Beverly to order her own flowers is a nice character touch.

jokes.text: Larry offers Paula his ATM password to pay for the flowers. Paula: 'I have it.' Larry: 'Well, no, I just changed it.' Paula: 'It's Leno now, right?'
jokes.setup: Earlier, Phil guessed that Larry changed his password from 'LARRY' to 'SANDERS'
jokes.punchline: Paula reveals the new password is 'LENO' — Larry's rival and industry anxiety made his ATM password
jokes.explanation: The episode's best joke and one of the finest closing gags in the series. It pays off the entire ATM password thread (LARRY → SANDERS → ?) with the perfect character-specific answer: LENO. Larry's password is his rival's name — simultaneously revealing his obsession, his paranoia, and his competitive fixation in a single word. The joke works on multiple levels: it's funny as a punchline, devastating as character insight, and perfectly summarizes the show's satirical project. The economy is extraordinary — one word does everything. This is an 8+ by any standard.

tmdb_overview: Larry's dad pays a visit to California, but Larry doesn't want to see him, so he adds that little chore to the things an already fed-up Beverly has to cope with.
